verdict: OK to lend in Nashik engineering & capital goods — pursue export-linked and power/T&D component makers with order-book visibility; avoid EPC contractors with long cash cycles and thin-margin casters.
title: Nashik Engineering & Capital Goods: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What this business physically is
**Nashik engineering runs on metal in, machined part out, and cash back only after the buyer accepts.** The units here are component makers, casting/machining shops and light capital-goods fabricators feeding auto, power transmission, railways and increasingly data-centre and export buyers [4]. Value sits in the order book and the machining tolerance, not in the shed. Cash sits in receivables and work-in-progress; the working-capital cycle is the whole game, and rating work is explicit that a longer cycle means more funding need and weaker liquidity [9]. **So when a proposal lands, check the receivable days and inventory days against the order book; if receivables are stretching past the stated credit terms, ask which buyer and why.**

## What has changed now
**The demand signal is genuinely strong and it is national, not local.** IIP for NIC 28 (machinery) is +10.3% YoY and +10.4% Apr-to-date [D], and engineering exports are +19.8% Apr-to-date in USD [D]. Maharashtra GST collections are running +8.6% Apr-to-date against India's +6.1% [D], so the state is pulling slightly ahead. Locally, a multinational has committed a large investment in a Nashik project [1] and Nashik industries have opened a Taiwan partnership route for technology and export business [3]. **Treat [1] and [3] as local news, not confirmed order flow — they tell us buyers are circling, not that your borrower has a purchase order.**

## Where the growth is — and who to avoid
**Pursue the component and structure makers riding power T&D, exports and data-centre demand.** Skipper posted its highest-ever Q2 revenue with PAT up 56% and record order book with strong export growth [6]; Pitti is commissioning a Hyderabad casting and machining facility backed by order visibility from data centres, mining, off-highway and railways [4]; DEE's order book crossed Rs 1,300 crore with Q3 revenue up 77% to Rs 286.7 crore [5]. **Avoid, for now, the pure EPC contractor and the undifferentiated caster.** Suzlon grew revenue 26% to Rs 4,869 crore but EBITDA stayed flat at Rs 720 crore and margin fell to 14.8% from 18.6% [7] — volume without margin. CRISIL notes EPC cash conversion cycles stay high versus OEMs [11]. **So when an EPC proposal lands, check whether margins are holding as volumes rise; if revenue is growing but EBITDA is flat, ask for the price-escalation clause.**

## How to grow safely
**Structure against the order book, not the balance sheet.** Take monthly stock-and-receivable statements, monthly order-book position with buyer names, and quarterly GST returns matched to sales. Ask for the bank-guarantee line separately — bidding guarantees are a real working-capital drag in this trade [9]. **If the borrower's top three buyers exceed half of sales, ask for the buyer-wise ageing every month.**

## Early-warning signs
**Watch receivable days first, margin second.** If receivable days cross the stated credit terms for two consecutive months, cut the drawing power. If EBITDA margin slips while revenue rises — the Suzlon pattern [7] — reprice or exit. If order book falls below six months of run-rate sales, ask for the pipeline. **Note the local sources are thin on Nashik-specific order data; collect from customer the city-level order book and buyer concentration before sanctioning.**
watch: Receivable days exceed stated credit terms for 2 months -> cut drawing power
Order book below 6 months of run-rate sales -> ask for pipeline, freeze enhancement
Margin falls while revenue rises -> reprice or exit
GST turnover trails book sales by more than 10% -> investigate, hold disbursement
Top 3 buyers exceed 50% of sales -> require buyer-wise ageing and credit insurance
